 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise NEA issued notices to 10 Singapore-registered firms over regional haze under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, asking for company links, land locations and fire-prevention details.
 Shares in First Resources and Bumitama Agri fell after the news, while Wilmar, Golden Agri-Resources and others said they would cooperate and provide the requested documents.
 The law, introduced in 2014, can fine offenders up to "$100,000 a day" and the haze is linked to illegal slash-and-burn fires in Indonesia's forests and plantations.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – Shares of Singapore-listed palm oil producers First Resources and Bumitama Agri fell in early trading on Oct 26 before recovering some ground by market close.
 They were among 10 Singapore-registered companies that received notices from the National Environment Agency (NEA) after the market closed on Oct 23, seeking documents and information on the transboundary haze affecting the region.
 First Resources shares fell 1.09% , or four cents, to close at $3.64 on Oct 26, from $3.68 on Oct 23.
 Bumitama Agri shares declined 1.84% , or three cents, to $1.60, from their previous closing price of $1.63.
 Besides First Resources and Bumitama Agri, the companies that were served notices include Wilmar International, Indofood Agri Resources, Kencana Agri, Golden Agri International, Asia Pulp & Paper Company, Asia Pulp & Paper Company (China), TSH Global Plantation and TSH Oversea.
 Golden Agri International is a subsidiary of Singapore Exchange (SGX)-listed Golden Agri-Resources, while TSH Global Plantation and TSH Oversea are linked to plantation group TSH Resources, which has a primary listing in Malaysia and a secondary listing in Singapore.
 Wilmar International shares fell 0.9% to close at $3.31, while Golden Agri-Resources rose 1.85% to 28 cents. Kencana Agri shares declined 5.66% to 50 cents.
 Shares of Indofood Agri Resources and TSH Resources remained unchanged.
 NEA said on Oct 23 that it had issued notices to 10 Singapore-registered companies under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA).
 The notices require the companies to provide information about their corporate relationships, locations of their land concessions in Indonesia, and measures taken to prevent and combat fires to facilitate investigations.
 Some of the companies named by NEA have since issued statements addressing the notices.
 Wilmar International was the first to announce its plan to comply with the directive from NEA on Oct 23. This was about three hours after the agency announced that it had issued the legal notices.
 A spokesperson for Wilmar later told The Straits Times that it is working to provide the relevant documents and information, and will give more details when there are material updates.
 First Resources said in its filing on Oct 24 that it has agreed to provide the necessary details.
 Subsequently, Bumitama Agri and its subsidiaries said in a filing on Oct 24 that the company will provide the requested documents and information to NEA.

 Golden Agri-Resources also said on Oct 24 that its Singapore subsidiary Golden Agri International had received the NEA notice and will cooperate with the government agency.
 Meanwhile, Indofood Agri Resources said on Oct 25 that it received a notice from NEA requiring it to provide documents and information. The company said it will make further announcements as and when there are material developments.
 Kencana Agri said on Oct 25 that it received a notice from NEA on the same day “requesting certain documents and information”, adding that it would cooperate fully with NEA in accordance with applicable laws.
 TSH Resources said on Oct 26 that its Singapore-incorporated subsidiaries, TSH Oversea and TSH Global Plantation, received notices from NEA on Oct 23 requiring them to provide documents and information by Nov 2.
 TSH Resources said it was reviewing the notices and would engage with NEA.
 Introduced in September 2014, the THPA targets those responsible for causing or condoning fires, and can be activated if the haze causes the Pollutant Standards Index, which measures air quality in Singapore, to stay in the unhealthy range in any part of the island for 24 hours or more.
 Those found guilty under the Act can be fined up to $100,000 a day, with the total capped at $2 million.
 The current haze is caused by fires raging in forests and plantations in Indonesia, primarily in Kalimantan and Sumatra. 
 The blazes are sparked by slash-and-burn practices to clear land. Such practices are illegal in Indonesia, but are still carried out as they are cheaper than removing trees using excavators.
